title: The Burghers of Calais
text:
In 1346, after his victory at Crecy, Edward III of England laid siege to the French port of Calais. The town held out for eleven months, until its people were starving. When it finally offered to surrender, Edward, angry at the long resistance, at first wanted to put everyone to the sword.

The chronicler Jean Froissart tells how, after his advisers urged mercy, Edward set a condition. He would spare the town if six of its leading citizens came out bareheaded and barefoot, with ropes around their necks, carrying the keys of the town and castle, to be put to death.

When the terms were read out in the market square, Eustache de Saint-Pierre, one of the richest men in Calais, stepped forward first and offered himself. Five others followed.

The six came out to the English camp as required, and Edward ordered them beheaded. His knights pleaded for them, and Edward refused. Then Queen Philippa, who was pregnant, knelt before him and begged him, for her sake, to spare them. Froissart says the king looked at her for a while in silence, and then gave the men to her. She had them clothed and fed and sent them away safe.
lesson: Leadership can mean offering yourself first when your community is in danger. Mercy, too, takes courage when anger is in charge.
people: Edward III, Queen Philippa of Hainault, Eustache de Saint-Pierre
caveat: Some historians think the scene was a planned ritual of submission rather than a real threat of execution.
